# Loopiter

> A lightweight, model-agnostic feedback loop for production AI systems.

Loopiter is an MIT-licensed software development kit for Node.js 22 and 24 and for Python 3.11+. The libraries capture executions and feedback, analyze scored segments, evaluate immutable candidates, and coordinate approval, deployment, or rollback through adapters the application owns. A fresh self-hosted init records autonomous mode and self-improving on. The worker spends only with --enable and follows plan.mode unless --mode is set. Constructing ImprovementController without a mode stays on recommend. An autonomous target is an exact prompt or routing key. The Node validator also accepts agent_release. Python accepts prompt and routing only. JsonFileStore, the Vercel AI SDK wrapper, and the OpenTelemetry exporter are Node-only. Loopiter is a library. It is not a hosted service, a model, a trainer, or an agent runtime. The core has no runtime dependencies and sends no telemetry. Published alpha: npm `0.3.0-alpha.1` (the alpha dist-tag; latest is `0.2.0-alpha.1`), Python `0.3.0a1`. Those published archives predate the self-hosted init and worker in this repository. The landing page introduces the SDK. A hosted console is separate from this library.

Source code: https://github.com/SanaanKhalid/loopiter

## Pages

- [Home](https://loopiter.co/): SDK console, the feedback loop, graduated autonomy, and links to the manifesto and blog.
- [Manifesto](https://loopiter.co/manifesto): Why a useful correction should start an improvement attempt, and what the application still decides.
- [Blog](https://loopiter.co/blog): Notes on evaluation and feedback loops.
- [Self-improving AI agents need a feedback loop you can evaluate](https://loopiter.co/blog/self-improving-ai-agents-need-a-feedback-loop-you-can-evaluate): What self-improving agents change, why an outside check matters, and which parts of that loop this SDK implements.
- [Graduated autonomy for self-improving AI agents: observe, recommend, experiment, autonomous](https://loopiter.co/blog/graduated-autonomy-for-self-improving-ai-agents): The four controller modes, why a fresh init records autonomous mode, and how gating, activation, and rollback work in Node.js and Python.

## Documentation

Canonical documentation is hosted separately from this site.

- [Overview](https://loopiter.docs.buildwithfern.com/get-started/overview): Capture, verified feedback, evaluation, approval, deployment, and rollback.
- [Supported capabilities](https://loopiter.docs.buildwithfern.com/get-started/supported-capabilities): What the Node.js and Python alphas include, and what they leave to the application.
- [Autonomy modes](https://loopiter.docs.buildwithfern.com/closing-the-loop/opt-in-autonomous-improvement): Observe, recommend, experiment, and autonomous modes.
- [Evaluation and deployment](https://loopiter.docs.buildwithfern.com/closing-the-loop/evaluation-and-deployment): Immutable candidates, holdout partitions, receipts, and rollback.
- [Agent systems](https://loopiter.docs.buildwithfern.com/closing-the-loop/agent-systems): Recording turns and tool calls without treating the SDK as an agent runtime.
- [Fine-tuning boundaries](https://loopiter.docs.buildwithfern.com/closing-the-loop/fine-tuning): The alpha does not train or fine-tune a model.
